scenes: It's almost three in the morning. A Sunday, in November, 1907. In a private library in New York City, more than a hundred bankers are waiting. They're tired. They want to go home. And the door… is locked. The man who owns the library has the key in his pocket. And nobody's leaving, until they save the country.

To see how it came to that, you need to know one thing about America back then. There was no Federal Reserve. No central bank at all. If a bank ran short of cash, there was nobody to call. And a newer kind of bank, called a trust company, was running very short. A regular national bank kept about a quarter of its deposits on hand, in cash. The trusts? About a nickel on the dollar.

Then came the spark. In October, two brothers named Heinze tried to corner the stock of a company called United Copper. On Monday, the stock jumped from 39 dollars to 52. On Tuesday, it touched almost 60… and closed at 30. By Wednesday, it was 10. The scheme was dead. And people started asking a dangerous question. Which banks were tied to those men?

One answer was the Knickerbocker Trust. One of the biggest trust companies in New York. On the morning of October 22nd, the crowd came for its money… and kept coming. In under three hours, the Knickerbocker paid out about 8 million dollars. A little after noon, it shut its doors. Now the fear had a life of its own. If the Knickerbocker could fall, so could anybody. So the lines moved down the street, to the next trust. And the next.

With no central bank, the job fell to one private citizen. J. P. Morgan. Seventy years old. He had his men go through the books of the next trust in line, overnight. When they told him it was sound, he said, "This is the place to stop the trouble, then." The next day, the trouble reached the Stock Exchange. Its president walked in around one-thirty, and said they'd have to close early. Morgan called in the bank presidents, and told them he needed 25 million dollars. In ten minutes. By sixteen minutes past two, they had pledged twenty-three point six. The exchange stayed open.

But the runs kept coming. And that brings us back to the library. Morgan put the trust company men in one room, and told them, you are going to put up another 25 million… to save each other. They held out most of the night. At about a quarter to five in the morning, their leader signed. Then the rest. Morgan unlocked the door. And the worst of the panic was over.

But here's the part that changed the country. Everybody understood how close it had been. The whole financial system of the United States had rested on one seventy-year-old man… and a locked door. So what happens next time, when he's not there? Morgan died in the spring of 1913. That same year, two days before Christmas, Congress passed the Federal Reserve Act. A central bank, built so the country would never again need one man to hold the key. Whether it's worked… is a story for another day. Subscribe, and we'll tell it. Along with everything from animal facts, to history's greatest battles, to the world's craziest financial collapses.
